source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR)
finding: Without outside feedback, asking a model to review and fix its own answer does not help reasoning and often hurts. The gains in earlier papers came from using the true label to decide when to stop.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback
limits: Prompts follow Kim et al. 2023; HotpotQA sample is only 100; prompt and temperature matter (see c14). 2023-era models.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2: revise only from real output, never from the model's own opinion of its answer.

source: Huang et al. (2024) same paper, oracle-label condition
finding: When the true label tells the loop whether to continue, self-correction looks great. This is the setting earlier positive papers used. It is not a real self-correction setting.
numbers: Oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CSQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, CSQA 82.0 to 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0.
limits: The label stops the loop on correct answers so they are never damaged; that is most of the effect.
agent_relevance: The gain is the value of a reliable check, not of reflection. Our S5 must get its signal from code or tests.

source: Huang et al. (2024) same paper, sections 4-5: debate vs self-consistency, and Self-Refine prompt audit
finding: Multi-agent debate (Du et al. setup, full GSM8K test set, 3 agents, 2 rounds) is only slightly better than self-consistency with 3 responses and clearly worse than self-consistency with 9 responses. Self-Refine's CommonGen-Hard gain came from a weak initial prompt: with a stronger initial prompt, self-correction lowered the score.
numbers: CommonGen-Hard: Madaan baseline 44.0 and refined 67.0 (their prompts); Huang's own stronger baseline 81.8 vs 75.1 after self-correct (table columns garbled in text extraction; check the PDF before quoting). Debate exact figures not copied.
limits: Table partly lost in extraction.
agent_relevance: If we use several attempts, a vote across samples is the fair comparator; any debate or critique step must beat it at equal calls.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs (TACL)
finding: Survey with a stricter lens. Findings: (1) no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except on tasks exceptionally suited to it; (2) it works well where reliable external feedback exists; (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables it. The bottleneck is feedback generation, not refinement.
numbers: Qualitative. Table 4 lists prior studies using oracle information or weak initial prompts (unfair settings).
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Survey; relies on others' numbers.
agent_relevance: Gives a checklist for fair tests: strong initial prompt, no oracle, matched compute. Apply it to our S5 tests.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) same paper, where it works
finding: Prompted self-feedback helps when the answer decomposes into parts that are each easy to check (for example constrained generation with listed constraints). It is a task property, not a general model skill.
numbers: No single number.
limits: Decomposability reading is the authors' judgement.
agent_relevance: Make self-feedback reliable by checking each constraint separately. Links to Decomposition (Fermi-ize).

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: One model generates, critiques and rewrites. Large gains on style-like tasks, almost none on math. The headline average is driven by preference-style tasks.
numbers: Abstract: about 20% absolute average gain over one-step generation across 7 tasks (GPT-3.5, GPT-4). Math Reasoning (GSM8K) 64.1 to 64.1 (0 change) in the main table. Oracle feedback on math: GPT-3 +4.8, GPT-4 +0.7 (appendix H.1). Code optimization with GPT-4 +8.7 absolute.
quote: The modest performance gains in Math Reasoning can be traced back to the inability to accurately identify
limits: Fuzzy goals are judged by the same model family; Huang and Kamoi show the initial prompt was weak. Math feedback often says the answer looks fine.
agent_relevance: Self-feedback is polish, not correctness. Keep it out of S5 for factual or logical tasks.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: The agent gets a real signal after each trial (environment result, unit tests), writes a short verbal reflection, stores it in memory, and retries. Gains are large, but the signal is external or test-based.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%. ALFWorld: ReAct+Reflexion completed 130 of 134 tasks. Gains over baselines: +22% ALFWorld (12 steps), +20% HotpotQA, +11% HumanEval. Test false-positive rate (passes tests but wrong) 16.3% on MBPP Python vs 1.4% on HumanEval Python.
limits: The HotpotQA runs used ground-truth correctness as signal (Huang flags this); self-written tests can pass wrong code.
agent_relevance: This is G2: revise from real output. Reflection text kept as memory between tries; the check must be a test, not the model's opinion.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing (ICLR)
finding: The model checks its output with tools (search, code interpreter, toxicity API) and then revises. Tool feedback gives reliable gains; the same loop without tools gives much less.
numbers: ChatGPT: +7.7 F1 over three QA tasks, +7.0% absolute over three math tasks, 79.2% reduction in toxicity probability. Ablation 'CRITIC w/o Tool' is below full CRITIC in every column shown (for example 42.0 vs 50.0, and 58.3 vs 64.9, in one QA table). Needs only three correction rounds.
quote: exclusive reliance on self-correction without external feedback may yield modest improvements or even deteriorate performance
limits: Authors write that self-correction alone may give modest gains or even hurt. Greedy decoding with cached search results.
agent_relevance: Clean evidence that the verifier, not the rewrite, carries the value. Matches the schema rule that checks are code.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (Findings ACL)
finding: Splits self-correction into finding the mistake and fixing it. Finding is the weak part. Given the first-error step, models fix traces well. New dataset BIG-Bench Mistake: 2186 CoT traces from PaLM 2 Unicorn with the first-error location marked.
numbers: Mistake finding: GPT-4 best, only 52.87 overall accuracy with direct step prompting. Backtracking with oracle location (correct traces ruined / wrong traces fixed, points): word sorting -11.11 / +23.53; multistep arithmetic -6.67 / +43.92 vs random location -6.67 / +20.39; Dyck -11.43 / +36.86 vs random -13.33 / +21.57. A small trained classifier beats prompting a large model at finding mistakes.
limits: Five BIG-Bench tasks; traces from one generator; location oracle rarely available.
agent_relevance: Supports step-level checks instead of 'is the whole answer right?'. S5 design: localize first, then resample from that step.

source: Stechly, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong: iterative prompting for reasoning problems
finding: On graph colouring, GPT-4 as its own verifier accepts almost nothing, so self-critique makes results worse. Even with a perfect external verifier, the content of the criticism matters little; the gain comes from having more tries.
numbers: No backprompt baseline 16% of 100 instances. LLM self-critique backprompting: 1 of 100 solved. Sound verifier: near 40%; binary vs single-error vs full-error feedback differences insignificant. Verification test: of 100 optimal colourings it accepted 2; of 500 colourings (118 correct) it accepted 30 and was right 5 times.
limits: One task, one model (GPT-4, 2023). Authors argue the success is the right answer being among top-k samples.
agent_relevance: A loop's gain may just be resampling. Compare against best-of-n at equal calls.

source: Valmeekam, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) Can LLMs Really Improve by Self-critiquing Their Own Plans?
finding: In Blocksworld planning, GPT-4 as verifier lets many bad plans through. Self-critique helps somewhat over one shot but a sound verifier helps far more. Feedback detail barely matters.
numbers: Plan accuracy: generator only 40/100; LLM+LLM backprompting 55/100 (3.48 iterations); LLM+VAL sound verifier 88/100 (4.18). LLM verifier accuracy 61/100; 38 of 45 invalid plans were accepted as valid (84.45% false-positive rate); 1 of 55 valid plans rejected. Feedback types on 50 instances: binary 37/50, plus first error 43/50, plus all errors 43/50.
limits: One domain, GPT-4, 100 instances.
agent_relevance: Verifier false positives end the loop wrongly. Use sound code checks (G2).

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
finding: Base Gemini 1.5 Flash gets worse on its second try on MATH. Multi-turn RL on self-generated data makes it better. Supervised fine-tuning on correction traces fails through distribution mismatch or behaviour collapse.
numbers: MATH500, Gemini 1.5 Flash: base acc@t1 52.6, acc@t2 41.4 (delta -11.2). Self-Refine 52.8 to 51.8 (-1.0). STaR 53.6 to 54.0 (+0.4). Pair-SFT 52.4 to 54.2 (+1.8). SCoRe 60.0 to 64.4 (+4.4). Base model changes 15.8% of answers in one direction and 4.6% in the other; the net -11.2 implies 15.8% is correct-to-incorrect. Abstract: self-correction gain +15.6% MATH, +9.1% HumanEval over base.
limits: Training, not a scaffold; Gemini models only. Column labels ic/ci were ambiguous in extraction, direction inferred from the net delta.
agent_relevance: Self-correction can be trained, so a scaffold on a frontier model should not assume it. Report acc@t1, acc@t2, delta in our harness.

source: Qu et al. (2024) Recursive Introspection (RISE): Teaching Language Model Agents How to Self-Improve
finding: Fine-tuning a model on its own multi-turn rollouts with reward supervision gives steady gains per turn on maths. GPT-3.5 prompting alone gains little over five turns.
numbers: GSM8K over 5 turns: LLaMa2-7B +17.7%, Mistral-7B +23.9%; per-iteration gains LLaMa3-8B +8.2%, Mistral +6.6% on own data. GPT-3.5 only +4.6%. MATH: LLaMa2-7B +4.6%, Mistral-7B +11.1%. Transfers between MATH and GSM8K.
limits: Fine-tuned small models; majority vote across turns, so part of the gain is extra sampling.
agent_relevance: Second proof that the skill is trained, not free. Not usable in a no-training scaffold.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Large Language Models Have Intrinsic Self-Correction Ability
finding: Disputes Huang. Says two factors decide whether intrinsic self-correction works: zero temperature and a fair (neutral) feedback prompt. Biased prompts push the model to change answers.
numbers: Six datasets, three prompt sets, several LLMs: with unbiased prompt and zero temperature all evaluated models improved (their Table 2). Higher temperature lowers accuracy during correction for GPT-3.5. Qwen 2.5 size ablation in Table 3. Per-dataset deltas not copied.
limits: Partial failed replication of Huang, mostly on easier benchmarks; gains modest.
agent_relevance: Use deterministic decoding and a neutral prompt in S5, then measure; do not trust it.

source: Li et al. (2024) Confidence Matters: Revisiting Intrinsic Self-Correction Capabilities of LLMs
finding: Proposes the If-or-Else (IoE) prompt: 'if you are very confident, keep your answer; otherwise update'. This reduces flipping of correct answers, the main failure in Huang.
numbers: Figure 1 compares Huang's Critical Prompt with IoE; final answer is output directly when the standard and IoE answers match. Numeric tables not extracted this session.
limits: Method read; no per-dataset numbers copied.
agent_relevance: A keep-by-default rule: change only when a check fails.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Understanding the Dark Side of LLMs' Intrinsic Self-Correction (ACL)
finding: Self-correction prompts make models waver: they change answers repeatedly, overturn correct ones, and show human-like biases on complex tasks. Two fixes help: put the original question last, and small fine-tuning.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo changes 81.3% of answers more than 6 times in a 10-round self-correction chat (3270 samples). Llama-3.1-8B on a complex task: -20.4% accuracy, 58.8% of correct answers overturned. Failure split in the agent task: overthinking 17.6%, cognitive overload 33.3%, perfectionism bias 49.0%. Question-repeating: accuracy +3.2 to +4.9, failure rate -5.3 to -10.9 points.
limits: ChatGPT, Llama, DeepSeek; probing only on the open model.
agent_relevance: Fix the round cap in code (about 3); put the original question at the end of the revise prompt.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Small Language Models Need Strong Verifiers to Self-Correct Reasoning (Findings ACL)
finding: Small LMs (up to 13B) can learn self-correction from their own critiques written with the correct solution as a hint (SCORE pipeline), but gains are notable mainly when a strong GPT-4-based verifier decides when to correct. A weak self-verifier limits benefit.
numbers: Five math and commonsense datasets, two models (abstract). Per-dataset deltas not extracted.
limits: Training method.
agent_relevance: The verifier must be stronger than the generator or external code.

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench: the Self-Correction Blind Spot (COLM)
finding: Same error, different attribution. Models fix the error when it is user-attributed and miss it when it is in their own earlier output. Appending 'Wait' removes most of the gap with no training.
numbers: 14 open non-reasoning models: average blind spot 64.5%. Fine-tuning on 5,306 error-correction traces cuts it by 76.0%. Appending 'Wait' cuts it by 89.3% and raises mean accuracy by 156%. Of what a model misses in its own natural errors, 4.3% to 10.8% is caught when shown as external. External errors trigger 179.5% more correction markers on GSM8K-SC.
quote: Appending Wait requires no training yet reduces the blind spot by 89.3%
limits: Open non-reasoning models only; reasoning models less affected. Three-judge agreement 95.0% on 238 samples.
agent_relevance: Present the draft to the checker as someone else's text and cue with 'Wait'. Cheap trick to test in S5.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling (budget forcing)
finding: Suppressing the end-of-thinking token and appending 'Wait' forces the model to re-check. Accuracy rises with more such rounds.
numbers: AIME24: s1-32B 50.0 without budget forcing, 56.7 with it (text: 50% to 57%). MATH500 92.6 to 93.0. Abstract: extrapolation beyond the model's limit by up to 27% on MATH and AIME24.
limits: Small model fine-tuned on 1,000 examples; benefit tied to extra thinking compute, not clearly correction.
agent_relevance: A bounded forced re-check lever for S5. Links to Test-time compute scaling and Overthinking.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via RL
finding: With reward only on final answers, R1-Zero learned to reflect and verify on its own, with a visible rise in the word 'wait' (the 'aha moment'). Reflection emerged from RL, not prompting.
numbers: Qualitative: reflection and revision behaviours grow as thinking length grows during training. Benchmark scores not copied.
limits: Behaviour shown for an intermediate checkpoint; whether 'wait' causes correction is not tested here (see c18, c19).
agent_relevance: Reasoning-trained models self-correct inside the trace; our scaffold adds external checks rather than duplicating this.

source: Weng et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Better Reasoners with Self-Verification
finding: Backward verification: treat the answer as given, mask a condition in the question, ask the model to recover it, and rank candidate answers by match. Reported small average gains across reasoning sets.
numbers: Text reports an average increase of about 2.33% on part of the tasks; table rows partly garbled, exact conditions not confirmed.
limits: Older models (GPT-3 era); small gains; same model verifies.
agent_relevance: Backward substitution is a cheap code-friendly check pattern.

source: Pan et al. (2024) Automatically Correcting LLMs: Surveying the Landscape of Self-Correction Strategies (TACL)
finding: Survey of training-time, generation-time and post-hoc correction by feedback source (self, human, tools, other models). Downloaded, not read this session.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Pointer only.
agent_relevance: Taxonomy for sorting our methods by feedback source.

source: Kim, Baldi, McAleer (2023) Language Models can Solve Computer Tasks (RCI)
finding: Recursive criticise-and-improve for web tasks. Huang notes its gains used ground-truth signals. Known only through Huang and Kamoi.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Secondary description only.
agent_relevance: Treat reported gains as oracle-assisted.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning through Multiagent Debate
finding: Several instances answer, read each other's answers and revise. Reported gains on GSM8K; Huang's full-test replication found no edge over self-consistency (c03).
numbers: Original used 100 GSM8K examples; replication used the full test set.
limits: Original not opened.
agent_relevance: Price any debate against majority vote.

source: Cross-study pattern 2022-2026 (synthesis of c01 to c20)
finding: The same split recurs. It helps with external or code feedback (Reflexion tests, CRITIC tools, VAL solver), with step-location oracles (Tyen) and after training (SCoRe, RISE). It fails or harms with prompted self-judgment alone (Huang, Stechly, Valmeekam). Disputed middle: neutral prompt plus zero temperature (Liu), keep-clause (Li), role-switch plus 'Wait' (Tsui).
numbers: Blocksworld 40 (one shot) to 55 (self-critique) vs 88 (sound verifier); graph colouring ~40% with sound verifier vs 1% with self-critique; Gemini Flash MATH base -11.2 vs SCoRe +4.4.
limits: Synthesis by this agent from the cited lines.
agent_relevance: S5 rule: the signal must come from outside the draft's author (code, tests, retrieval); the model only writes the repair.

source: Agent-loop patterns built on self-correction (Reflexion, CRITIC, Tyen backtracking)
finding: Three patterns used in agent loops: (1) reflect-and-retry with verbal memory plus a test (Reflexion); (2) verify with a tool then revise (CRITIC, three rounds); (3) regenerate from the first wrong step (Tyen backtracking).
numbers: CRITIC: three correction rounds. Tyen: re-generate the step at temperature 1 until it differs from the original, at most 8 tries.
limits: Round caps are part of the design; Zhang (c16) shows long loops waver.
agent_relevance: Template for an S5 operator: locate, resample that step, re-check with code, cap rounds near 3.

source: Fair-evaluation checklist for self-correction (Kamoi section 8, Huang recommendations, SCoRe metrics)
finding: To test a self-correction scaffold fairly: strongest first-attempt prompt, no oracle labels, report how often right answers get broken and wrong ones fixed, match compute against resampling.
numbers: Metrics to log: acc@t1, acc@t2, delta, right-to-wrong rate, wrong-to-right rate, plus best-of-n at equal calls.
limits: Checklist assembled from the cited papers.
agent_relevance: Add these numbers to the harness output for any S5 arm.
